name: Iridology

image.caption: Iridology iris eye chart left mirror

lead: Iridology is an alternative-medicine practice in which a practitioner examines the colour, fibres and markings of the iris and reads them against a chart that maps zones of the iris to organs and body systems. Practitioners then suggest dietary changes, supplements or cleanses aimed at the organ areas they identify.

paras: A session typically involves a close look at the eyes with a magnifier, torch, camera or slit lamp, comparison with an iris chart, and a recommendation of nutrition, detox or lifestyle changes. Some people in wellness and looksmaxxing circles use it as a first step before skin, digestion or energy protocols, on the idea that internal congestion shows up in complexion and appearance.

Blinded studies have found that iridologists cannot reliably identify disease from iris photographs, and ophthalmology reviews warn that false reassurance or false alarms may delay proper diagnosis or lead to unnecessary treatments or costly cleanses. The practice is unlicensed in most places and the eye itself is not touched, so there is no direct physical risk from the examination.

chain: Iris chart is read for organ 'weaknesses'
Practitioner recommends diet, supplement or cleanse changes
Believers expect clearer skin, energy and a healthier look
angle.text: Practitioners present iris reading as a way to spot internal imbalances that they believe show up in complexion, hair and vitality, then guide a nutrition or detox plan. The link to appearance runs entirely through the follow-up plan rather than the examination itself.

lead: Iridology (also iridodiagnosis) is a diagnostic practice within naturopathy and holistic health that studies the iris of the eye. Practitioners divide each iris into dozens of zones on a chart, each corresponding to an organ or body region, and interpret pigment spots, fibre density, crypts and rings as signs of strength, inflammation or toxicity in the matching area.[1][2]

In appearance-focused communities it is mentioned as a way of working out which internal system to address first when skin, hair or energy seem off, with the follow-on plan usually being a diet change, supplement or cleanse. Proponents hold that the iris is linked to the body through the nervous system and develops alongside other tissues, so that it works as a map of the whole body.[1]

Controlled studies since 1979 have tested whether iridologists can identify specific conditions from iris images. Systematic reviews and a 2026 ophthalmology position paper report that diagnostic accuracy has not been shown, while a minority of reviewers argue that more rigorous studies are still warranted.[3][4][5][6]
infobox: Ignaz von Peczely, Nils Liljequist, Bernard Jensen
Not licensed by government agencies in the US or Canada

paras: Iridology charts typically divide the iris into some 60 to 90 zones arranged like a clock face, with the left iris mapping the left side of the body and the right iris the right side; chart details differ between schools.[1][2] Practitioners look at pigment patterns, lacunae and crypts, radial lines and contraction rings, and distinguish inherited structural features from marks said to be acquired through lifestyle.[1]
Some schools also classify iris colour into constitutional types: blue and grey irises as lymphatic, brown as haematogenic and mixed as biliary, each linked to different predispositions.[1]

Descriptions of reading the eye for illness reach back centuries; a 1665 work by Philippus Meyeus is often cited as an early statement of iris principles.[2] The modern practice is credited to the Hungarian physician Ignaz von Peczely, whose popular origin story involves an injured owl, an account his own nephew later called apocryphal.[2] Swedish clergyman Nils Liljequist published an iris atlas in 1893.[2]

In the early 1900s Emanuel Felke in Germany described further iris signs, and from the 1950s the American chiropractor Bernard Jensen taught classes and promoted iridology in the United States, linking it with natural foods and detoxification.[2] The practice is offered mainly by naturopaths and holistic practitioners, with certification courses from private organisations.[1][2]

An assessment can be done in person with a magnifier or slit lamp, or from photographs. The practitioner compares findings with a chart and may offer recommendations on nutrition, supplements or cleansing programmes.[1] Digital iris images are also used in research projects that apply machine learning to iris features for conditions such as coronary artery disease; these studies are separate from traditional chart reading.[7]

In a 1979 JAMA study, three iridologists examined iris photographs of 143 people, 48 of whom had kidney disease, and could not distinguish those with kidney impairment from those without.[8][2] A 1988 BMJ study asked five iridologists to identify gallbladder disease from iris slides of 39 patients awaiting surgery and controls, and found they could not do so reliably; the investigator later described how participants' beliefs shifted after seeing such results.[9][6]

A 1999 systematic review located four blinded case-control studies and judged that the majority did not support iridology as a diagnostic method.[3] A 2005 prospective case-control study examined whether an iridologist could detect cancer susceptibility in 110 people and reported no diagnostic value.[10][2] A German controlled study asked the same question about colorectal cancer in 29 patients and controls.[11] A 2008 literature review of 25 publications from 1970 to 2005 found 15 in favour of the method and 10 against, and called for studies with greater methodological rigour.[4]

A 2026 position paper from an ophthalmology patients' association reviewed the history, proposed mechanisms and trials and concluded that iridology cannot be supported as a diagnostic or screening tool.[5] A 2015 Australian government review of therapies for private insurance rebates found no clear evidence of effectiveness for iridology.[2]

Proponents say the iris forms from the same embryonic tissues as the rest of the body and is wired to it by nerves, so that changes in organs are reflected in iris markings before symptoms appear.[1] Iridology is promoted as non-invasive and preventive.

Researchers and clinicians respond that the iris is largely structurally stable after infancy, which is the property used by iris-recognition biometrics, and that no anatomical pathway linking iris zones to organs has been demonstrated.[2][5]

Authors of reviews in ophthalmology and allergy note that inaccurate readings can produce false reassurance that delays real diagnosis, or false alarms that lead to unneeded treatment and expense.[5][12] An Archives of Ophthalmology commentary described the practice as potentially harmful for these reasons.[13]

Ignaz von Peczely publishes early iris charts, per Grokipedia.[1]
Nils Liljequist publishes an iris atlas.[2]
Bernard Jensen popularises iridology in the United States.[2]
JAMA study finds iridologists cannot identify kidney disease from iris photographs.[8][2]
BMJ gallbladder study reports similar results.[9]
